cls: Antiviral - deoxynucleoside analogue DNA polymerase inhibitor (acyclovir prodrug)
quick: Herpes zoster: 1 gram three times daily for 7 days
May be taken with or without food; maintain adequate hydration
Decades of data show no increased birth-defect risk; treat when indicated
Acyclovir is excreted in milk but considered compatible
Dose reduction required by CrCl - risk of renal precipitation/AKI
No specific dose adjustment generally required
Renal function and hydration; neurologic status in elderly/renal impairment
summary: Valacyclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir with much higher oral bioavailability, allowing less frequent dosing. After absorption it is rapidly converted to acyclovir, which is selectively activated in herpes-infected cells. It is used to treat cold sores, genital herpes (treatment, suppression, and reduction of transmission), and herpes zoster (shingles), and chickenpox in children. It requires renal dose adjustment and adequate hydration.
indications: Cold sores (herpes labialis) in adults and adolescents >=12 years
Genital herpes: initial and recurrent episodes, chronic suppression, and reduction of transmission in immunocompetent (and HIV-1-infected for suppression) adults
Chickenpox (varicella) in pediatric patients aged 2 to <18 years

dosage.n: For 7 days; start within 48 h of rash onset
For 1 day; start at earliest symptom (tingling/itch/burn)
For 10 days; best within 48 h of onset
For 3 days; start at first sign/symptom

dosage.d: 1 gram once daily (500 mg once daily if <=9 recurrences/year)
20 mg/kg three times daily (max 1 gram per dose)

admin: May be taken with or without food
Maintain adequate hydration to reduce risk of renal precipitation of acyclovir
Begin therapy at the earliest sign or symptom (prodrome) for best efficacy
An oral suspension (25 or 50 mg/mL) can be compounded from 500 mg tablets for children unable to take tablets
moa: Valacyclovir is rapidly and almost completely converted to acyclovir (and L-valine) after oral absorption. Acyclovir is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to acyclovir monophosphate, then to the active triphosphate by cellular enzymes. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase by competitive inhibition, chain termination after incorporation into viral DNA, and inactivation of the polymerase. It is selective for herpes-infected cells.

absolute: Clinically significant hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous adverse reactions) to valacyclovir, acyclovir, or any component
relative: Immunocompromised (risk of TTP/HUS at high doses)

preg: Decades of clinical data with valacyclovir and its metabolite acyclovir in pregnant women have not identified a drug-associated risk of major birth defects. Untreated genital HSV poses real risks to the fetus/neonate. Treat during pregnancy when indicated; benefits generally outweigh risk.
lact: Acyclovir (the active metabolite) is excreted into breast milk but infant exposure is low relative to therapeutic pediatric doses; valacyclovir is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Requires dose reduction based on creatinine clearance for all indications; reduce dose and/or lengthen the interval in renal impairment and ensure adequate hydration to prevent crystalluria and acute kidney injury. Hemodialysis removes acyclovir; dose after dialysis.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is generally needed; transient ALT elevations have been reported uncommonly.

moderate: Probenecid and cimetidine (reduce acyclovir renal clearance, raise levels)
minor: Drugs competing for active renal tubular secretion may increase acyclovir exposure
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate BUN and serum creatinine; rare ALT elevation

serious: Acute renal failure / crystalluria (especially dehydration or renal impairment)
CNS effects (confusion, hallucinations, agitation, tremor) - especially elderly/renal impairment
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / hemolytic uremic syndrome (immunocompromised, high dose)
rare: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, TEN)

monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, BUN), especially in elderly or renal impairment
Neurologic symptoms (confusion, hallucinations) in elderly/renal impairment
CBC and signs of TTP/HUS in immunocompromised patients on high-dose therapy
counsel: Start treatment as early as possible when symptoms begin (tingling, itching, burning)
Drink plenty of fluids while taking this medicine
Complete the entire course even if you feel better
It reduces symptoms and (for genital herpes) transmission risk but does not cure herpes; continue safer-sex practices
Report confusion, reduced urination, severe fatigue, or unusual bruising/bleeding
pk: Rapidly converted to acyclovir after absorption; clinical benefit greatest if started early
Acyclovir plasma peak approximately 1.5 to 2 hours after an oral dose
Acyclovir half-life approximately 2.5 to 3.3 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Higher bioavailability (~55%) than acyclovir allows less frequent (1-3 times daily) dosing
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); compounded suspension refrigerated per pharmacy directions
pearls: Prodrug of acyclovir with ~3-5x higher oral bioavailability, enabling simpler dosing schedules
TTP/HUS has occurred with very high doses (e.g., 8 g/day) in immunocompromised patients
Adequate hydration and renal dose adjustment are key to preventing nephrotoxicity
One-day 2 g BID regimen is convenient for cold sores; start at the prodromal tingle
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember, then continue your regular schedule. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not double up.
overdose: Overdose (often from accumulation in renal impairment) may precipitate acyclovir in the renal tubules, causing acute renal failure and anuria, and may cause agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and seizures. Management is supportive with hydration; hemodialysis effectively removes acyclovir and may be used in severe cases or acute renal failure.
